stem: Which of the following describes **research and development (R&D)**?

options.content: Technical work to invent or improve the firm's products
options.rationale: Correct: R&D creates and improves products and methods.

options.content: Collecting views from customers on the existing price
options.rationale: That is market research.

options.content: Training sales staff to speak to customers politely
options.rationale: That is training, not R&D.

options.content: Advertising the products on the radio and in newspapers
options.rationale: That is promotion.

explanation: R&D is the scientific and technical work behind new products and processes.

stem: Which stage of product development comes immediately after **idea generation**?

options.content: Screening of the ideas
options.rationale: Correct: weak ideas are removed before money is spent.

options.content: Launch of the product
options.rationale: Launch comes near the end.

options.content: Review of sales results
options.rationale: Review is the last stage.

options.content: Testing the product with customers
options.rationale: Testing follows development.

explanation: The order is idea generation, screening, development, testing, launch and review.

stem: What is the main purpose of **screening** new product ideas?

options.content: To launch every idea quickly before the rivals do
options.rationale: Screening reduces the number of ideas.

options.content: To patent each idea before it has been tested at all
options.rationale: A patent is not the aim of screening.

options.content: To drop weak ideas before costly development starts
options.rationale: Correct: this saves the money that development and testing would cost.

options.content: To increase the cost of the average product
options.rationale: Screening aims to cut waste.

explanation: Screening removes weak ideas early, because development and testing are expensive.

stem: Which of the following is a **source** of new product ideas from within a business?

options.content: Complaints printed in a national newspaper column
options.rationale: This is an external source.

options.content: A rival's new product on sale in the local shops
options.rationale: This is an external source.

options.content: An advertisement from a supplier of new materials
options.rationale: This is an external source.

options.content: Suggestions from sales staff who hear views
options.rationale: Correct: employees are an internal source of ideas.

explanation: Employees are an internal source; customers, competitors and suppliers are external.

stem: A fictional furniture firm in Gweru spends US\$24,000 on developing and launching a new chair. It expects a net cash inflow of US\$9,600 a year. What is the payback period, assuming the inflow arises evenly through each year?

options.content: 0.4 years
options.rationale: This divides the inflow by the cost.

options.content: 3.6 years
options.rationale: This adds the inflow to the cost before dividing.

options.content: 2.5 years
options.rationale: Correct: 24,000 ÷ 9,600 = 2.5 years.

options.content: 5 years
options.rationale: This is the life of the product, not the payback.

explanation: 24,000 ÷ 9,600 = 2.5 years, which is 2 years and 6 months.

stem: A fictional tuck-shop owner in Mutare invents a sweet with a new recipe but cannot afford a patent. Which risk is MOST likely?

options.content: The recipe will be protected for twenty years automatically
options.rationale: Protection needs a patent.

options.content: A larger firm may copy the recipe and sell it more cheaply
options.rationale: Correct: without protection the idea can be imitated.

options.content: Customers will refuse to buy any new sweet from her
options.rationale: There is no evidence of this.

options.content: The recipe will lose its value because it is too cheap
options.rationale: The cost of the recipe is not the issue.

explanation: Without a patent, competitors may copy an unprotected invention.

stem: Why do most products that reach the **launch** stage still carry a risk of failure?

options.content: Testing proves that every product will sell very well
options.rationale: Testing reduces risk, not removes it.

options.content: Launch is always done before any tests are ever made
options.rationale: Testing comes before launch.

options.content: All customers refuse to buy any new product at all
options.rationale: Customers do buy new products.

options.content: Testing cannot fully predict how all customers behave
options.rationale: Correct: customers' actual behaviour may differ from the test.

explanation: Tests use small samples and cannot fully predict the behaviour of the whole market or the reaction of competitors.
hints: What are the limits of a test?

stem: A fictional small bakery has US\$8,000 of spare cash. A consultant says it should spend all of it on R&D for a new type of bread. Which statement is the BEST evaluation?

options.content: R&D always gives a firm a large profit within a year or two
options.rationale: R&D is uncertain and slow.

options.content: The risk is high for a small firm, so a cheap trial is wiser
options.rationale: Correct: the firm is small and the result is uncertain.

options.content: R&D is useless for any bakery and never helps it at all
options.rationale: R&D can help, but scale and risk matter.

options.content: The spare cash has no other use that the firm could ever try
options.rationale: Cash has other uses (an opportunity cost).

explanation: A small firm could lose all its spare cash, so low-cost testing of ideas is a more cautious approach.
hints: Think about the size of the firm and the uncertainty of results.

stem: Employees can be a source of ideas for new products.
explanation: True. Sales and production staff often see problems and opportunities that managers do not.

stem: A patent stops competitors from making any similar product.
explanation: False. A patent protects a specific invention for a limited time, but competitors may develop a different way to do the same job.

stem: Match each stage of product development to what happens in it.

right.content: Designing the product and making a prototype
Trying the product with customers and for quality
Rejecting ideas that are unsuitable or too costly

explanation: Each stage has a different job in reducing risk and cost.

stem: Choose the correct word for each gap.

payload.template: A {{blank:a}} gives the owner of an invention the legal right to stop others using it for a limited period, and a {{blank:b}} is the first working model of a product.

explanation: A patent protects an invention; a prototype is a first working model.

stem: A fictional cosmetics firm in Bulawayo generates 150 new product ideas in a year. Six are launched. What percentage of ideas reached the launch stage? Give the answer to one decimal place.
explanation: 6 ÷ 150 × 100 = 4.0%. Inverting the fraction gives 25.

stem: The cosmetics firm spends US\$90,000 a year on developing new products. Six are launched, but only three are still selling after two years. Calculate the development cost for each lasting product.
explanation: 90,000 ÷ 3 = US\$30,000 per lasting product. Dividing by the six launched gives US\$15,000, which ignores the failures.
workedSolution: 1. 90,000 ÷ 3 = US\$30,000 per lasting product. Dividing by the six launched gives US\$15,000, which ignores the failures.
hints: Divide by the number of products that last, not the number launched.

stem: A fictional mining-supplies firm in Kadoma spends US\$52,000 on developing and launching a safety helmet. It expects net cash inflows of US\$13,000 a year for six years, and nothing after that. Calculate the total net gain over the six years (total inflows minus the cost).
explanation: Total inflows = 13,000 × 6 = US\$78,000. Net gain = 78,000 − 52,000 = US\$26,000. (Payback is 4 years.) US\$78,000 is the inflow before taking away the cost.

stem: Name the legal right that protects an invention from being copied for a limited period.
explanation: A patent.

stem: Explain **one** reason why a business should develop new products.

points.description: Existing products will reach the decline stage
New products replace falling sales
So the business can keep revenue and avoid depending on one product

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Existing products will eventually reach the decline stage and their sales will fall. New products replace this lost revenue, so the business does not depend on a single product.

explanation: A reason developed to its effect.
hints: Think about the life of a product.

stem: A fictional dairy in Gweru wants ideas for a new type of yoghurt. Explain **two** sources of ideas it could use.

points.description: Customer surveys or comments
Application: customers may ask for lower-sugar or larger packs
Employees, especially sales staff
Application: delivery drivers hear shop owners' requests

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The dairy could survey its customers, who may ask for a lower-sugar yoghurt or larger packs. It could also ask its employees: delivery drivers hear shop owners' requests every day and can pass on ideas.

explanation: Two sources, each applied.
hints: Choose two different sources and link each to yoghurt.

stem: Analyse why testing a product before launch can reduce the risk of failure.

points.description: Testing shows how real customers react
Faults in design or safety can be found and corrected
The firm can adjust price or promotion
So the firm avoids spending on a full launch of a product that may not sell

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Testing shows how real customers react and finds faults in design or safety that can be corrected. The firm can also adjust the price or promotion before launch, so it avoids spending a large sum on launching a product that will not sell.

explanation: A chain from testing to reduced risk.
hints: Link what testing finds to the cost of a full launch.

stem: A fictional farm-equipment maker in Chinhoyi is considering spending a third of its profit each year on R&D. Evaluate this decision.

points.description: R&D can produce unique products that sell at higher prices
Patents could protect the products for a time
Over time R&D can lower costs through better processes
It is costly and uncertain; results may take years and may fail
Less profit is available to pay owners or invest elsewhere
Judgement with reason, e.g. worthwhile if competitors are innovating and cash is sufficient

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: R&D can produce unique products that sell at higher prices and can lower costs through better processes, and patents could protect them for a time. However, it is costly and uncertain, results may take years, and a third of profit reduces what is available for owners or other investment. It is worthwhile if competitors are innovating and the firm has enough cash to survive a failure; otherwise a smaller budget is wiser.

explanation: A balanced evaluation with a condition.
hints: Weigh the long-term benefit against the cost and risk.

stem:
A fictional software start-up in Harare spends US\$60,000 on developing a payroll app. The expected net cash inflows are:

| Year | Net cash inflow (US\$) |
| --- | ---: |
| Year 1 | 15,000 |
| Year 2 | 20,000 |
| Year 3 | 20,000 |
| Year 4 | 20,000 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the payback period in years (assume the inflow arises evenly within each year).
parts.explanation: After year 1: 60,000 − 15,000 = 45,000 left; after year 2: 25,000 left; after year 3: 5,000 left. Year 4 inflow is 20,000, so 5,000 ÷ 20,000 = 0.25. Payback = 3.25 years.
parts.workedSolution: 1. After year 1: 60,000 − 15,000 = 45,000 left; after year 2: 25,000 left; after year 3: 5,000 left. Year 4 inflow is 20,000, so 5,000 ÷ 20,000 = 0.25. Payback = 3.25 years.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the total net gain over four years (total inflows minus the development cost).

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State **two** risks of developing the app.

points.description: Customers may not buy it, so the inflows would be lower than forecast
A competitor may launch a similar or better app

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Customers may not buy it, so the inflows would be lower than forecast, and a competitor may launch a similar or better app.

parts.explanation: Two risks of a new product.

explanation: Payback 3.25 years; net gain US\$15,000; the forecasts and competitors create risk.
hints: Subtract each year's inflow from the cost until it is repaid.

stem: Read the extract. Dube Seeds is a fictional company in Gweru that has sold the same maize seed for eight years. Sales have fallen by 10% a year as rivals offer drought-resistant seed. The managing director proposes to spend US\$120,000 on R&D to develop its own drought-resistant seed, which would take about three years. The finance director says the firm could instead buy the right to sell a rival's seed under licence.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain **one** benefit to Dube Seeds of developing its own seed.

points.description: The firm would own a unique product
It could patent or protect the new seed
So it could charge a higher price and avoid paying licence fees

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The firm would own a unique drought-resistant seed which it could protect, so it could charge a higher price and avoid paying licence fees to a rival.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Assess whether Dube Seeds should carry out the R&D or buy the licence.

points.description: R&D gives ownership and potentially higher long-term profit
R&D costs US\$120,000 and takes three years, while sales fall
The result is uncertain and may fail
A licence gives a product sooner and with less risk
But the licence costs fees and depends on the rival
Judgement with reason, e.g. licence now, R&D later if cash allows

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Developing its own seed would give Dube Seeds a product it owns and could protect, with higher long-term profit. But it costs US\$120,000, takes three years while sales keep falling, and might fail. A licence brings a product sooner with less risk, though fees reduce profit and the firm depends on a rival. Dube Seeds should probably take the licence now to stop the fall in sales and start R&D later if it has the cash.

parts.explanation: Own product against speed and risk.

explanation: R&D gives ownership but is slow, costly and risky; a licence is quick but dependent on a rival.
hints: Compare the time, cost and certainty of each option.
